factText: The scaly-foot snail is metal - literally! These snails live on deep sea hydrothermal vents, and build iron plate armour on their shell and soft tissue. They're the only animals known to utilize iron sulphide in this way.
imgCredit: Nakamura K., Watanabe H., Miyazaki J., et al. (CC BY 2.5)

factText: Bird lungs are strange. Instead of pumping air in and out of a sack (terribly inefficient), their lungs are more like a tube where air can flow constantly in one direction. There is evidence that some dinosaur lungs are also like this.
Gherkin slug - They're only found in New Zealand, and eat fungi and algae.
Hellraiser mite - The long spikes probably offer protection from predators.
Tadpole shrimp - native to NZ, these have existed since the dinosaurs first appeared. They're capable of reproducing without males (through parthenogenesis).
Frosted phoenix moth - Endemic to NZ. This species was not seen for 65 years, and feared extinct, before a Swedish tourist just... found one at his hotel one day.
Velvet worms, or Peripatus - They are actually ferocious predators that have existed before the dinosaurs. They shoot glue to capture prey.
There used to be many species of dwarf elephants. There's a chance the origin of the cyclops in mythology may be from people discovering small elephant skulls!

Some caecelians (a type of amphibian that looks like a worm) scrape off their mother's skin to eat. She fills it with nutrients, so it's kind of like their way of nursing. This species is bright yellow!
The caterpillars of the gum leaf skeletoniser (what a great name for a moth) keep their old head case when they molt, and stack them up on their head for some reason.
Beyond pest cockroaches, there are thousands of roach species, many of which are rare and boast pretty colours. Some roaches secrete milk to feed young, like mammals.

Dodder or amarbel - This type of plant has almost entirely lost the ability to photosynthesize. They don't even have roots when mature. Instead, they are entirely parasitic and can invade other plants' vascular systems.

Wood rose, or pua o te rēinga - Endemic to NZ. This parasitic plant cannot photosynthesize, and is entirely dependent on taking nutrients from the roots of other plants. Their flowers are only pollinated by NZ's terrestrial bats (and potentially the kakapō).
Ghost pipe - Many fungi exchange nutrients with trees; the ghost pipe interferes, and takes the nutrients for itself. They cannot photosynthesize, and range in colour from white to deep red.

Ramisyllis kingghidorahi - This is a type of worm with a branching body; it has one head and multiple butts. The worm lives in sponges, but each branch is able to grow eyes, break off and swim away to reproduce. And yes, it's named after King Ghidorah.

factText: Broad-tailed paradise whydah - Male paradise whydahs have truly maxxed out their tails, though they drop the giant feathers outside of breeding season. These birds are also brood parasites (lay eggs in other birds' nests).
Marvelous spatuletail - Males grow beautiful 'rackets' on the ends of their long tail feathers, and display these in their courtship dance.
Pennant-winged nightjar - During the breeding season, males of this nocturnal bird grow these incredible pennants, which can be more than 40cm long.
Standard-winged nightjar - Breeding males grow giant, flag-like wing feathers. These trail above the bird when he flies, like a pair of kites.
On dry days, tree trunks will actually shrink slightly, as their vessels that transport water can collapse inward by a tiny amount.
A large tree can transport over 400L of water from their roots to leaves every day - without using any energy input!
The largest compartment of a cow's stomach - the rumen - has a volume of up to 200L. You could almost fit a large Auckland Council recycling bin in one!

The word 'tree' just describes a plant that is vaguely tree-shaped. Trees have independently evolved probably hundreds of times. For example, the island of Santa Cruz has a type of daisy that has evolved into a tree 20m tall.
Termites are a type of roach, and unrelated to ants. While worker ants only include genetically female individuals, termite workers can be female or male.
Boring sponge - These are called boring sponges because they bore holes into rock or shellfish where they grow (not because they're boring!) One has even been found growing on the back of a crab.
African painted dogs sneeze as a way to vote whether to go on a hunt.

Greenland sharks smell like pee - they have very high concentrations of urea in their flesh, which also makes them toxic. These sharks may live up to 400 years, and require 150 years to reach maturity.
Leaf sheep - This type of sea slug is able to store chloroplasts from the algae it eats, a process called kleptoplasty. This gives it the ability to photosynthesize!
